keyTakeaways: The problem is not whether a team says subtitles, surtitles, or captions; the risk is building the wrong workflow because the word was never defined.
For non-English Fringe shows, audience-facing copy may say English subtitles, but production planning should usually specify prepared English surtitles cued live by an operator.
Captions are often an access commitment: they may need dialogue, speaker information, music, sound effects, and off-stage audio, not just translated lines.
Projection Mode and mobile viewer delivery are delivery decisions, not content definitions; they only work well after the team knows what text it is preparing.
When terminology is clear, SurtitleLive setup becomes easier: language tracks, projection, mobile viewing, operator cueing, blackout, and recovery can be configured around the real audience need.

faq.question: What is the terminology trap for non-English shows at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival?
faq.answer: A company may ask for subtitles, a venue may hear captions, a translator may prepare surtitles, and a stage manager may need live cue control. Each word can imply a different workflow, so the team should define the text, delivery method, and live operation before setup.

faq.question: Can we say English subtitles in audience-facing marketing?
faq.answer: Yes. Many audiences understand the phrase English subtitles. For production planning, it is usually better to specify prepared English surtitles if the text is a reviewed translation cued live during a performance.

faq.question: What is the difference between surtitles and captions in theatre?
faq.answer: Surtitles usually mean prepared translation text for a live performance in another language. Captions usually support access to spoken and sound information, including dialogue, speaker identification, off-stage sounds, music, or effects.

faq.question: Are projection and mobile viewing the same decision as surtitles or captions?
faq.answer: No. Projection and mobile viewing are delivery methods. Surtitles and captions describe what kind of text is being prepared. A show can use translation surtitles by projection, by mobile viewer, or by both.

faq.question: How does clear terminology help SurtitleLive setup?
faq.answer: Once the team knows whether it is preparing translation surtitles, access captions, or both, it can decide which language tracks to enable, whether to use Projection Mode, mobile viewer delivery, or both, and what the operator needs to cue live.

faq.question: What should a small Fringe team ask for instead of just subtitles?
faq.answer: A clearer request is: prepared English surtitles for a live non-English show, cued by an operator, delivered by Projection Mode, mobile viewer, or both. If captioning access is required, plan sound and speaker information separately.

glossary.definition: Prepared text shown during a live performance, usually to translate a show performed in another language.
Text that represents dialogue and relevant sound information, often used to support D/deaf or hard-of-hearing audiences.
A familiar audience-facing term for translated or transcribed text, more common in film and video but often used casually for live theatre.
A term closely related to surtitles, often used in opera and some North American contexts for text shown above or near the stage.
Captions visible only to audience members who choose to use them, often on a personal device such as a smartphone or tablet.
A browser-based audience view opened by QR code or link, allowing each audience member to read an enabled language on their own device.
A display mode intended for theatre screens or projectors, used when the venue supports shared visible text.
The live process of advancing prepared text in time with the performance, including holding, jumping, or hiding text when needed.
